purpose: Pacritinib is used to treat a serious bone marrow disease called myelofibrosis, which causes scarring in the bone marrow and problems with blood cell production. It is especially used for patients who have low platelet counts, meaning their blood does not clot well. This medicine helps reduce an enlarged spleen and relieve symptoms like fatigue, night sweats, and bone pain.
how_it_works: Your bone marrow disease is driven by overactive proteins called JAK2 and IRAK1 that send too many wrong signals inside your cells, causing problems. Pacritinib works by blocking these proteins, like turning off a faulty switch, so those harmful signals are reduced. This helps your bone marrow work better and can shrink your spleen and ease your symptoms.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, low platelet counts (which can increase bleeding risk), low red blood cell counts (anemia), swelling in your legs or feet, tiredness, and bruising more easily than normal.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious bleeding, including bleeding in the brain or stomach, so tell your doctor right away if you have unusual bruising, blood in your stool, or a bad headache. It can also cause heart rhythm problems, so let your doctor know if you feel your heart racing or fluttering. Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm the baby. It may also raise your risk of serious infections, so avoid people who are sick and report any fever promptly.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 200 mg taken by mouth twice a day, about 12 hours apart, with or without food. Try to take it at the same times each day. Swallow the capsules whole — do not crush or open them. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how you respond and any side effects you experience.
